items.consigne: In English, infer why Mei is preparing to leave. Identify two clues and connect them to your idea. Do not claim where she is going unless the text supports it.
items.stimulus: The violin case was already beside the front door. Mei checked the concert schedule on the fridge, then began to put on her shoes. 'I'll warm up at the hall,' she told her brother.
items.reponse_attendue: Mei may be leaving to prepare for a performance or rehearsal. The violin case is by the door, and she checks a concert schedule and says she will warm up at the hall. Those details suggest music practice is her purpose. The exact event is not certain.
criteres: An unstated but text-compatible purpose is inferred, not merely a copied fact.
At least two actual details are accurately quoted or paraphrased.
The reason links the case/schedule/warm-up to a possible music activity; no invented facts.
items.feedback: If the response says only “She puts on shoes,” ask what the case and schedule suggest. If it asserts she won a competition, ask for a supporting line: none is present.

items.consigne: What is one reasonable unstated reason Ari asks Kim to check the address? Justify with one or more text clues.
items.stimulus: Ari looked at the large envelope addressed to the school office. 'Did you check the address?' Ari asked. Kim nodded and read the label aloud. Ari placed the envelope in the outgoing mail tray.
items.reponse_attendue: Ari probably wants the envelope to reach the correct place. Ari asks whether the address was checked, Kim reads the label, and Ari mails it only afterward. The text does not say the address was previously wrong.
criteres: Infers a reasonable motive beyond the exact wording.
Cites the checking of address before posting as evidence.
Explains why checking then posting suggests attention to delivery accuracy.
items.feedback: If the learner states the envelope contained money or a secret, redirect to what is actually written; its contents are unknown.

items.consigne: Infer a possible reason the organizers ask for two clips. Give a clue and explain why your answer is plausible; do not assert the weather.
items.stimulus: **Outdoor art display:** Please attach each drawing with two clips. The display boards stand beside the open courtyard. Extra clips are in the red container at the entrance.
items.reponse_attendue: They may want drawings to stay attached securely outdoors. The instructions require two clips and say the boards stand in an open courtyard. Extra clips at the entrance support that fastening matters. Wind is a possibility, not a stated fact.
criteres: Infers a purpose rather than repeating the two-clip instruction.
Uses the open courtyard plus clip instructions as evidence.
Does not present wind or bad weather as certain.
items.feedback: “There is a storm” is unsupported. Replace it with “The display might need to stay secure because it is outside.”

items.consigne: What can you reasonably infer about Theo’s decision? Use the dog’s behaviour and Theo’s action as clues. State one thing we cannot know.
items.stimulus: The family dog paused near the steps. It lifted its front paw and took a few slow steps. Theo watched, then fetched the leash and called an adult rather than starting the usual long walk.
items.reponse_attendue: Theo may be concerned that the dog is uncomfortable or injured: the dog lifts its paw and walks slowly, and Theo calls an adult instead of starting the long walk. We cannot diagnose an injury or its cause from the passage.
criteres: Infers possible concern or precaution from observed text, not a medical diagnosis.
Names an animal-behaviour clue and a Theo-action clue.
Acknowledges a clear limit of what is known.
items.feedback: If the child claims the dog broke a bone, ask what the story actually establishes; the cause and diagnosis are not given.

items.consigne: Infer why Rowan changed the sign. Include evidence from before and after the change and explain what the details imply.
items.stimulus: At the start of the market, the price sign lay face down behind the stall. By the first break, Rowan had written the item names and prices in thick letters. When customers arrived, Rowan leaned the sign against a box facing the walkway.
items.reponse_attendue: Rowan may want people walking by to understand what is for sale and its price. At first the sign is face down, then Rowan writes names and prices in thick letters and faces it toward the walkway. Those changes make the information easier to see. The text does not establish whether sales increased.
criteres: Unstated communication purpose is plausible.
Uses the initial position and later lettering/direction as evidence.
Explains how the change could help readers, without inventing outcomes.
items.feedback: If the answer only says “Rowan wrote prices,” ask what that change might achieve for passing customers.

items.consigne: What intention might explain both the guide at Door B and the arrow sign? Give two clues and a logical connection.
items.stimulus: **Museum floor update:** Visitors may enter the exhibit through Door B while the main entrance is being painted. A guide is stationed at Door B from 10 a.m. until noon. An arrow sign is also posted at the regular entrance.
items.reponse_attendue: Staff likely want visitors to find the temporary entrance without confusion. The main entrance is being painted, there is a guide at Door B, and an arrow sign at the old entrance directs visitors. Nothing says the museum is fully closed.
criteres: Infers an unstated purpose shared by the two measures.
Uses the guide, arrow and entrance-change details accurately.
Connects the signs to wayfinding while rejecting a full-closure claim.
items.feedback: If the learner says “The museum is closed,” point to “visitors may enter ... through Door B.”

items.consigne: Infer why Jo changes strategy. Explain the inference with two separate details; avoid claiming what Jo feels as a fact.
items.stimulus: When the group began the puzzle, Jo insisted on sorting the blue pieces. Half an hour later, the middle of the puzzle was still empty. Jo looked at the picture on the box, pushed a few blue pieces aside, and began to look for pieces with straight edges.
items.reponse_attendue: Jo may decide that sorting by colour alone is not helping enough. The middle is still empty after half an hour, and Jo checks the box image before looking for straight-edged pieces. Changing to edges suggests trying a different way to make progress. The passage does not prove Jo is angry.
criteres: Identifies an unstated reason for a strategy change, not just the change itself.
Names slow progress and Jo’s new attention to edges/image.
Uses cautious language and avoids unsupported emotions.
items.feedback: If the student says “Jo is furious,” request exact emotional evidence; none is provided.

items.consigne: What are staff likely trying to prevent? Cite at least two clues and explain the implied purpose. Also state one fact the notice does NOT establish.
items.stimulus: **After the school fair:** Staff will wash the cafeteria floor at 4:30 p.m. The exit beside the cafeteria will be closed for thirty minutes. Visitors should use the doors across from the gym until the orange floor signs are removed.
items.reponse_attendue: They likely want people to avoid walking across a freshly washed floor, possibly to reduce slipping or tracking water. The floor is washed at 4:30, a nearby exit closes for thirty minutes, and floor signs remain until it is ready. The notice does not state that anyone has already slipped.
criteres: Purpose follows from floor cleaning, temporary closure and signs.
Two or more correct, specific details are linked in reasoning.
No unsupported claim about an actual accident.
items.feedback: If the answer says an accident occurred, distinguish preventing a risk from reporting an event.

items.consigne: Make TWO different inferences about why the leader wrote particular instructions. For EACH, cite a detail and explain the connection.
items.stimulus: **Nature club message:** The group will meet at 8:00 a.m. on Saturday, even if the path is damp. Bring a pencil, a notebook and shoes that can handle mud. The club leader will bring magnifying glasses for everyone. Please leave large backpacks at home.
items.reponse_attendue: Inference 1: The leader may expect wet or muddy ground, because the message mentions a damp path and shoes that handle mud. Inference 2: The leader may want members to travel light or avoid bulky bags on the route, because large backpacks should stay home while essential notebooks and shared magnifiers are listed. The trail’s exact width or difficulty is not given.
criteres: Two distinct unstated intentions or expectations are articulated.
Each inference is paired with a correct clue or combination of clues.
Each connection is explained without making the route’s hazard level certain.
items.feedback: If the two answers both say “muddy shoes,” request a genuinely new intention related to packing lightly; if a storm is asserted, note no storm is mentioned.

items.consigne: Offer TWO different inferences about the organizers’ priorities. Explain each with a different set of textual details; do not claim a past problem occurred.
items.stimulus: **Community radio booth note:** The microphone will be ready at 1:45 p.m. Speakers should test the volume before their segment begins at 2:00 p.m. Keep doors closed during the recording, but do not lock them. A sign outside will ask visitors to speak quietly near the booth.
items.reponse_attendue: Inference 1: Organizers likely want clear audio, because they ask for volume tests, quiet voices outside and doors closed during recording. Inference 2: They likely want people to be able to leave the booth safely, because the doors should stay closed but explicitly not locked. No previous accident is reported.
criteres: Provides distinct, plausible inferences for audio clarity and accessibility/exit.
Each has a specific clue set and a causal explanation.
Does not invent an emergency or an earlier noise complaint.
items.feedback: If the student calls the booth soundproof, ask for evidence: quiet-voice instructions show concern about noise, not guaranteed soundproofing.

items.consigne: INDIVIDUAL MASTERY PROOF A. Read the unseen STORY. Write TWO DIFFERENT inferences about Sam’s goals or reactions. For each, identify at least one precise text clue AND explain how it supports your inference. Do not simply repeat stated actions. You may mention uncertainty. No teacher hint selecting a clue or interpretation.
items.stimulus: On Saturday morning, Sam carried a small box into the community centre. A sign by the entrance read, 'Art display entries close at noon.' The clock above the desk showed 11:55. Sam stopped and asked the volunteer, 'Is there still a place for one more piece?' The volunteer pointed to an empty spot and handed Sam a label. Sam opened the box, placed a carefully folded paper star on the table and wrote a title on the label. On the way out, Sam glanced at the clock again, but walked toward the door much more slowly than before.
items.reponse_attendue: Inference A: Sam may worry about missing the display deadline or finding a space. Evidence: the noon deadline, the 11:55 clock and 'Is there still a place for one more piece?' Reasoning: the near deadline and direct question suggest urgency or concern about acceptance. Inference B: Sam may feel relieved after getting a place or may be less rushed. Evidence: the volunteer points to an empty spot and gives a label; Sam displays the star, then walks more slowly than before. Reasoning: after successfully entering the piece, Sam’s pace changes. Do not claim Sam won a prize or that a precise emotion is proven; other carefully justified readings can be credited.
criteres: First claim is an unstated, text-compatible inference about urgency/acceptance, with a precise clue and explicit reasoning.
Second claim is DISTINCT and plausible regarding change in urgency/reaction, with independently identifiable supporting words and reasoning.
Both claims avoid contradicting facts and avoid claiming unreported prize or outcome.
No guiding hints about answers; student identifies and connects clues independently.
items.feedback: If the learner lists “Sam placed a star” as an inference, ask on a later unseen passage what that fact suggests. If both answers are about the deadline, the second distinct inference is missing. No hints during scored attempt.

items.consigne: INDIVIDUAL MASTERY PROOF B. Read the unseen INFORMATIONAL NOTICE. Make TWO DIFFERENT inferences about the organizers’ intentions. For each inference, cite at least one specific clue and explain your reasoning. Do not invent visitor numbers or claim the start time changed. No highlighted clues, prompts to find the answer, or model text during the attempt.
items.stimulus:
**North Street Library — November program update (fictional notice)**
For November, the weekly story session will meet in the ground-floor hall instead of the upstairs room. The new hall has a step-free entrance and more space for strollers. Staff will place one sign at the main door and another near the old upstairs room. Story time will still begin at 10:00 a.m. Families can borrow books at the usual desk. During the first week, the library asks visitors to arrive a few minutes early.
items.reponse_attendue: Inference A: Staff may want story time to be easier to access for families using strollers or needing step-free entry. Evidence: the move to the ground-floor hall, its step-free entrance and extra stroller space. These improvements suggest an accessibility purpose, though no attendee’s circumstances are given. Inference B: Staff may want visitors to find the changed location without confusion. Evidence: signs at the main door and old room, plus the request to arrive early in the first week. These support a wayfinding/transition purpose. The notice states the 10:00 start remains unchanged. Alternative distinct interpretations are accepted if each is defensible with text and reasoning.
criteres: First claim proposes an unstated plausible reason for relocation/accessibility, using the hall/entrance/stroller details with a reasoned link.
Second claim offers a different intention about navigation or adjusting to the change, supported by the signs/early-arrival detail and reasoning.
Both inferences respect explicit facts (time unchanged, lending desk unchanged) and avoid invented participant characteristics.
No clue-selection help is supplied; performance documents independent reading across this new genre.
items.feedback: If the response says the session now starts later, reread “still begin at 10:00” after scoring and retrain with another notice. If two answers only repeat “the hall is downstairs,” ask for separate organizers’ aims on an alternate unseen text.
